abstract: Studies of spatially-resolved molecular gas in galaxies have been limited to low-z due to the time-consuming nature of targeting galaxies one-by-one. With Resolved Observations of CO Kinematics at COsmic noon (ROCOKCO), we aim to measure gas kinematics in high-z main-sequence field galaxies in the first unbiased and statistical sample. We employ an efficient multiplexing strategy by (1) choosing a field with a wealth of photometric and spectroscopic data to characterize galaxy properties; (2) searching for a high number of spec-z galaxies within a single Band 3 primary beam; and (3) ensuring the redshifts fit within a 3.75 GHz sideband and thus only require 1-2 spectral tunings. This strategy has uncovered 6 pointings which contain 24 z~1.5 galaxies, and an additional 66 with consistent photo-zs, covering a range of masses and IR luminosities; it is thus not biased to gas-rich galaxies. At 3kpc resolution we will constrain rotation curves, velocity dispersions, dynamical masses, baryon fractions, and kinematic asymmetries in the molecular gas. This will serve as a direct comparison to cluster galaxy samples, the next-generation hydro simulations, and state-of-the-art low-z surveys.

Dark matter is the backbone for evolving galaxies in a cosmological context but its interaction with baryons in the dense and rapidly evolving interstellar medium of high-z galaxies remains unclear. We propose a pilot study to map the CO(2-1) in three discs on the z~1.5 main seqeunce with dynamical measurements out to ~15 kpc from KMOS >100-hr observations at matched spatial resolution (0.5"), HST+JWST imaging and CANDELS photometry, and total gas fractions from NOEMA CO(2-1) spectra at 3". The requested deep Band 3 data will resolve the molecular gas extent and kinematics and, combined with this unique ancillary set, enable the first precise measurements of stellar, gas, and dark matter profiles at high redshift. This study will establish the properties of dark matter haloes in which distant discs reside and demonstrate the feasibility of extending the analysis to the parent sample with KMOS ultradeep and planned NOEMA low-resolution observations.

The importance of dark matter (DM) in high-z galaxies is debated with key implications for cosmological models of galaxy formation. Rotation curves (RCs) are a prime tool to study DM in galaxies but must be traced out to large radii where DM dominates over baryons. [CII] observations in individual galaxies at z=4-5 revealed the existence of rotating gas disks and allowed measuring their inner baryon-dominated RCs (R<3-4 kpc), while stacking [CII] experiments discovered diffuse [CII] emission extending out to 15 kpc in diameter. We propose ultradeep [CII] observations at 1.5 kpc resolution in two galaxies at z=4.5 that have (1) rotating gas disks, (2) evidence for extended [CII] emission, and (3) incoming JWST imaging. Our goals are to (1) study the gas kinematics in the outer regions to disentangle rotation from possible inflows or outflows, (2) trace extended RCs to unambiguously probe the DM halos, (3) measure the gas velocity dispersion at large radii and study disk stability. Our pilot ultradeep ALMA observations can open the only possible window to trace extended RCs at z>4, which will be otherwise inaccessible even for future facilities like SKA in HI and the ELT in H-alpha.

Studies of spatially-resolved molecular gas in galaxies have been limited to low-z due to the time-consuming nature of targeting galaxies one-by-one. We aim to measure spatially-resolved CO(2-1) kinematics in high-z main-sequence field galaxies with the first unbiased and statistical sample. We employ an efficient multiplexing strategy by (1) choosing a field with a wealth of photometric and spectroscopic data to characterize galaxy properties; (2) searching for a high number of spec-z galaxies within a single Band 3 primary beam; and (3) ensuring the redshifts fit within a 3.75 GHz sideband and thus only require 1-2 spectral tunings. This strategy has uncovered 6 pointings which contain 24 z~1.5 galaxies, and an additional 66 with consistent photometric redshifts, covering a range of stellar masses and infrared luminosities; it is thus not biased to gas-rich galaxies only. At a resolution of 3kpc, we will constrain rotation curves, velocity dispersions, dynamical masses, baryon fractions, and kinematic asymmetries in the molecular gas. This will serve as a direct comparison to z~1.6 cluster galaxy samples, the next-generation hydro simulations, and state-of-the-art low-z surveys.

We propose a deep and very high resolution (500 pc) observation of a main-sequence rotator at z=4.5. While the sub-kpc ISM structure in high-redshift starbursts/SMGs has been explored, normal z>4 systems remain an uncharted territory at this resolution. Because of its high surface brightness, its HST and planned JWST observations (COSMOS-Web), VC875 is by far the best candidate to start this type of observations. These observations will resolve the gas clouds, which are the seeds of star formation, and provide high quality dynamical information. We will: 1) reveal the small-scale ISM properties of VC875, detect giant molecular clouds, and measure their dynamical mass; 2) study the resolved Kennicutt-Schmidt relation; 3) probe the baryon cycle by detecting possible outflows and unveiling the nature of the [CII] halo of VC875; 4) measure from the dynamics the total mass distribution and its connection with the gas and stellar components. In addition, three lower-z (z=1.3,2.0, and 3.4) bright continuum sources are located in the same pointing, allowing for free very high-resolution comparisons of dust versus stellar morphologies, together with the local variations of dust attenuation.

We request multi-transition CO observations to measure accurate gas masses for a golden sample of 16 galaxies at z=4-5. These objects are representative of massive (M_star = 10^10-10^11 Msun), star-forming (SFR = 100-1000 Msun/yr), primeval galaxies. All of them have (1) ALMA [CII] data at sub-kpc resolutions providing the rotation curve and cold gas distribution, (2) JWST images providing the stellar mass distribution, and (3) VLA CO(1-0) data providing a first-order estimate of the gas mass. To break the disk-halo degeneracy between the gas contribution and the dark matter (DM) contribution, we need to estimate accurate gas masses, so the alpha_CO factor, for each individual galaxy. We will (1) construct CO SLEDs to measure alpha_CO and the gas mass, (2) fit rotation curves accounting for the contributions of gas, stars, and DM, (3) study the evolution of scaling laws (Tully-Fisher relation and more), (4) study star-formation laws using gas and star-formation-rate maps. Our project will exploit a unique ALMA+VLA+JWST synergy to measure the total mass content (gas, stars, and DM) of massive galaxies at z=4-5, tracing DM in a cosmic epoch that has been out of reach until now.
